recentItems.title: Breaking Down Beyoncé's B'Day...20 Years Later | The Rolling Stone Studio
recentItems.description:
20 years after the @beyonce delivered her pop masterpiece 'B'Day,' social media editor Elise Brisco and writer Larisha Paul head to The Rolling Stone Studio to discuss the superstar's sophomore project. #beyoncé 

On Beyoncé flexing her acting chops: "I want to say 'Irreplaceable' was honestly the video that kind of stuck out the most to me off bat. I feel like there's not as much narrative in pop videos [these days]. And she was really acting like her and that man they hired to play in this video was just like...they were going through this horrific breakup. And I was like, nobody wants to do a fake breakup for the cameras anymore. Just go and do the stuff, throw the stuff outside, throw the keys, snatch, do all the things. And I think she was just such a. And obviously she was leaning into her acting stuff a little bit more around this time."

On the influence that B'Day had on Beyoncé's discography: "It is so foundational to everything that we know and love and understand about Beyoncé now. I think we've obviously seen her come into this mastery of a certain kind of craftsmanship and skill and that goes on the production side, on who she's recruiting and the rooms that she's working in and how she's presenting it. Even the visual album stuff we mentioned before, but also just the way that she, the Beyonce, the experience live, all of that, the way she is kind of archiving her career starts with B'Day in a lot of ways. I think for me, it's like you don't get "Diva" without B'Day. You don't get "Don't Hurt Yourself" without B'Day. You don't get "Cuff It" without B'Day. Every single album that came after B'Day is rooted in that record so deeply."

On the 'B'Day' song that has stood the test of time: "I think the more time that I've spent with 'B'Day' throughout my life, "Get Me Bodied" is the most consistent probably out of all of them. I was hearing it at the family cookouts and the family reunions and the block parties. I think especially growing up and being in New York, being in the Bronx specifically, it was just one of those songs you could blast out your car and you're driving around. You're in the backseat of someone's car who's driving around and you're just kind of hearing it everywhere. But then I also think it lends itself to community in a very specific way of having this dance break moment."

recentItems.title: Olivia Rodrigo & Sarah McLachlan Talk Daisy Chain Fields Festival, Lilith Fair & More | Cover Story
recentItems.description:
Rolling Stone's exclusive digital cover story features four of the stars from @OliviaRodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields festival: @sarahmclachlan, Chappell Roan, Doechii, and Rodrigo herself. #sarahmclachlan, who founded the all-women festival Lilith Fair in 1997, joined #oliviarodrigo in a conversation on video, which also features Rolling Stone co-editor-in-chief Shirley Halperin and senior writer Angie Martoccio. Filmed in Los Angeles a few days before Daisy Chain, the interview discusses starting those two historic festivals, sexism in the industry, what they love about each other's music, and the power an all-women festival can have.

Rodrigo on Lilith Fair’s impact: “Something that's definitely not lost on me is how much times have changed … And I think that's in large part to the way that you broke down barriers, Sarah, and people of your generation, who really fought to be taken seriously and fought to have the same microphone and the same stage. I'm just endlessly grateful for that. I also feel like Daisy Chain is a celebration of how far we've come as women in music.”

Rodrigo on what she hopes for Daisy Chain: “Music was the first medium where the way I felt was really accepted. Growing up, that was my safe space. So if girls can come to Daisy Chain and feel a little sliver of that, that would be a dream.”

Rodrigo on Dolly Parton passing: “She's a saint, seriously. Talk about a pen, talk about a voice, talk about a heart. I am so saddened by her loss. I really appreciate how she never spoke badly about anyone. I really always appreciated that about her and wanted to be more like that myself. She even spoke about some crazy sort of bad individuals with just so much generosity and love, and I think we just need so much more of that in today's world, and she's just the best of us.”

McLachlan on Rodrigo calling her about Daisy Chain:  “Joy and elation in an instant. I was like, ‘Hallelujah! Someone is finally taking the torch and carrying it forward.’”

McLachlan on Rodrigo starting an all-women festival:  “I think you're brave to be at the forefront of something that is going to anger a lot of people. But fuck that, and good for you for standing up for it."

McLachlan on fighting for what’s right: “When someone says no to me, I just push back even harder to prove them wrong when it seems so simple and so ridiculous.”

Read the Rolling Stone cover story here: https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/olivia-rodrigo-daisy-chain-sarah-mclachlan-doechii-chappell-1235619725/
